description: Tsukumogami are Japanese yōkai born from discarded household objects — combs, umbrellas, teapots, or lanterns — that gain sentience after roughly a hundred years of service. Cast-off tools take animal or human forms and turn mischievous or vengeful toward neglectful owners. On Setasubun, the eve of the spring equinox, households sweep out old implements and burn them before they can awaken.
research_notes: Verified against Wikipedia and yokai references. The input's object sentience after ~100 years and the Setasubun burning custom are both accurate and folded in.

description: Xiezhi (獬豸) is the single-horned justice beast of Chinese tradition, usually pictured as a goat-, ox-, or lion-like animal with black fur. In accounts, when disputes were brought before it, it gored the guilty and spared the innocent, making it an emblem of impartial judgment. Its image decorated the robes of imperial censors and judges, and it passed into other East Asian legal symbolism.
research_notes: Standard figure of Chinese legal symbolism; folds in input appearance (horned beast), behavior (judging the guilty), and cultural significance (censor's emblem).

description: Mayohiga (迷い家) is a phantom house of Japanese mountain folklore, recorded in Yanagita Kunio's 1910 Tōno Monogatari. It appears at dusk on remote paths and in deep valleys; those who enter may take food or goods, and some return wealthy, while others who stay too long are never seen again. It is a supernatural dwelling tied to mountain spirits rather than a permanent place.
research_notes: Recorded in Tōno Monogatari; input's treasure-bestowing and vanishing themes preserved. Note that 'mayoiga' in modern use also refers to a different 'lost house' motif for lost children.

description: Mô-sîn-á (魔神仔), also romanized mo-sin-a or mosina, are small, hairy, nimble spirits of Taiwanese folklore, pictured as child- or monkey-like beings in mountains, forests, and wild country across the island's ethnic groups. They lead travelers astray, daze victims with illusions, and feed them filth disguised as food; remedies include shouting the lost person's name and making loud noises.
research_notes: Verified against folklorist Lin Mei-rong's Academia Sinica interview (魔神仔的人類學想像) and Chinese Wikipedia; input's 'small, hobbit-like' appearance, mischief, and pan-Taiwan distribution confirmed.

The entry appears to derive from conflation or modern invention.

description: Long (龍) is the Chinese dragon: a benevolent rain-bringer with a long serpentine body, antlers, four legs, and the power to fly without wings while controlling water, clouds, and weather. It dwells in rivers, lakes, seas, and sky, symbolizing imperial power, yang energy, and good fortune. Dragon dances, dragon-boat races, and rain prayers honor it.
research_notes: Well-documented Chinese mythological figure; input's wingless serpentine form, weather control, and auspicious significance all accurate.

description: Yagwanggwi (야광귀, 'night-light ghost') is a Korean folk spirit said to appear on the night of lunar New Year's Eve (seotdal geumeum), stealing people's shoes or sandals while they sleep. Documented by the National Folk Museum of Korea, the tradition holds that hanging a sieve or mesh by the door keeps the ghost away, because it stops to count the holes and is delayed until dawn.
research_notes: Verified against National Folk Museum of Korea documentation and Korean Wikipedia; input's shoe-stealing on lunar New Year's Eve and sieve-warding custom confirmed.

description: Yamawaro (山童) is a kappa-like mountain yōkai of western Japan, especially Kyūshū and the Chūgoku region, appearing as a small, hairy, childlike figure with a round head and sometimes a water dish on its crown. It is said to descend to rivers in spring and become a river kappa. It helps woodcutters haul logs when given rice cakes, and plays harmless tricks when gifts are withheld.
research_notes: Corrected input's 'Nagano mountains' attribution — yamawaro belongs to western Japan and Kyūshū (the Nagano mountain yōkai is yamabiko). Kyūshū origin, kappa connection, and log-carrying behavior confirmed.

description: Yuki-onna (雪女), the snow woman, is a yōkai of Japanese winter folklore: a beautiful, pale-skinned woman with long black hair and a white or blue kimono who appears in snowstorms. She lures travelers into the cold and freezes them with her breath, yet sometimes spares those who are brave, kind, or handsome. Lafcadio Hearn's retelling in Kwaidan, published in 1904, made her internationally famous.
research_notes: Well-documented yōkai; input's snowy habitat, freezing breath, and ice-like beauty confirmed. Hearn's Kwaidan connection added.

description: Yūrei are the restless ghosts of Japanese tradition, given their classic form in Edo-period art and kabuki: a woman with long black hair, a white funeral kimono, and trailing sleeves, rendered with pale or blue-tinted skin and no feet. They are souls with unfinished business who died with strong attachment or injustice. Edo woodblock prints, notably Maruyama Ōkyo's, fixed this enduring image.
research_notes: Verified Edo-period visual tradition; input's white kimono, black hair, and restless-soul behavior accurate. Maruyama Ōkyo's ghost painting noted.

description: Rokurokubi (轆轤首) is a Japanese yōkai that looks like an ordinary person, usually a woman, by day but whose neck stretches to surprising length at night, letting her head roam, spy, and lick lamp oil. Folklore warns that a person whose neck aches at night may be a rokurokubi; the head can be kept from rejoining the body if the neck or torso is hidden or blocked.
research_notes: Well-documented yōkai; input's stretching neck and spying behavior confirmed. Added the folk remedy of hiding the body to trap the head.

description: Gumiho (구미호) is the Korean nine-tailed fox, a fox that cultivates for a thousand years to grow nine tails and the power to take human form, most often a beautiful woman. In traditional tales she seduces men to feed on their livers or hearts, though later retellings give her redemptive and sympathetic roles. The gumiho appears in oral tales, in the Samguk Yusa, and in modern Korean drama and film.
research_notes: Verified against standard references; input's nine tails, seduction, and thousand-year cultivation confirmed.

description: Fenghuang (鳳凰) is the Chinese phoenix, a composite celestial bird often described with the head of a golden pheasant, the back of a tortoise, the neck of a snake, and the tail of a fish, its five colors carrying cosmic significance. It is said to appear only in times of peace and virtuous rule, and it pairs with the dragon as a symbol of yin, the empress, and marital harmony.
research_notes: Well-documented Chinese mythological bird; input's composite form, celestial status, and pairing with the dragon confirmed.

description: Not independently attested as a named dragon of Tibetan folklore. No source documents a 'Sang-ngag Gökhang' dragon; the name appears to conflate Tibetan terms — 'gsang sngags' (secret mantra) and 'dgon khang' (protector chapel). The recorded form matches the Tibetan dragon 'Druk', a weather-controlling serpent, but the specific name and claimed Bon prominence are unverified.
research_notes: Term analysis: gsang sngags = secret mantra, dgon khang = protector chapel; the documented Tibetan dragon is 'Druk'. 'Lung ta' prayer flags mean 'wind horse', not dragon. Marked unattested per policy; flagged for potential removal or correction to Druk.

description: Shidaidaka (次第高) is a yōkai reported in Shimane Prefecture and the Chūgoku region of Japan that grows taller and taller the longer a person looks up at it, looming ever higher over the viewer. The folk remedy is to look at it between one's legs, which either reveals it as small and harmless or makes it vanish. It is a classic yōkai that preys on human perception.
research_notes: Verified via Japanese yōkai databases (yokai.jp); the growing-with-the-gaze mechanic and the between-the-legs remedy are the standard account. Input's traits confirmed.

description: Not independently attested as a figure of Korean folklore. No source documents a 'Sonangi', a Jeju sea goddess who protects fishermen yet can sink boats. Documented Jeju sea deities include Yeongdeung Halmang, the wind-and-sea goddess honored in the February Yeongdeunggut rites, and Seolmundae Halmang, the giant creator goddess. The recorded traits likely conflate these attested figures.
research_notes: Searches returned no 'Sonangi' in Korean or English sources. Jeju's documented sea-goddess tradition centers on Yeongdeung Halmang (KHS intangible heritage listing) and Seolmundae Halmang. Marked unattested per policy; flagged for potential removal.

description: Sun Wukong (孫悟空), the Monkey King, is the trickster hero of the Ming-dynasty novel Journey to the West: a stone-born monkey with a magic staff that can grow to any size, somersault clouds, transformations, and hairs that create copies of himself. After rebelling against heaven, he guards the pilgrim Xuanzang westward, embodying wit, disobedience, and eventual enlightenment.
research_notes: One of the most famous figures in Chinese literature; input's combat prowess, transformations, and journey role confirmed.

description: Under the recorded name 'Jian', Chinese folk tradition documents jian spirits (魙/漸): 'ghosts of ghosts' that arise when dead souls die again into an even lower class of being. The concept, traced to the 13th century, combines the Tang apotropaic jian character with the idea that ghosts are mortal. The input's headless figure matches the separate wútóu guǐ (headless ghost) tradition.
research_notes: Jian spirits attested via Volchkova's Journal of Ethnology and Folkloristics article (2023); input's headless-ghost description is a different figure (wútóu guǐ). Name retained but description corrected to the documented concept; flagged for possible rename/split.

description: Jiangshi (殭屍) is the 'hopping corpse' of Chinese folklore: a reanimated body, often of a person whose breath failed to leave at death or whose grave was disturbed, moving in stiff, leaping bounds with arms outstretched. It drains life energy from the living and is warded off by mirrors, glutinous rice, rooster blood, and talismans.
research_notes: Well-documented Chinese undead figure; input's stiff hopping, arms-out form, and life-draining behavior confirmed, with standard folk countermeasures.

description: Jiǔwěihú (九尾狐), the nine-tailed fox of Chinese mythology, is a shapeshifting fox spirit that gains one new tail each century of cultivation. It often appears as a beautiful woman who seduces and corrupts rulers — famously Daji of the Shang dynasty — yet auspicious nine-tailed foxes also appear as omens in the Shanhaijing. It is the ancestor of the Korean gumiho and Japanese kitsune.
research_notes: Well-documented Chinese figure; input's nine tails, thousand-year cultivation, and seduction of rulers confirmed. Daji connection and later Korean/Japanese influence noted.

description: Not independently attested as a goddess of Chinese religion. No source documents a 'Jiuku Tiannu' (救苦天女) who descends during epidemics to cure disease. The name appears to conflate documented figures: Taiyi Jiuku Tianzun (太乙救苦天尊), the Daoist Lord of Salvation, and Jiutian Xuannü (九天玄女). Neither is attested as a plague-curing goddess under this name.
research_notes: Searches in Chinese and English found no '救苦天女'. Closest documented figures are Taiyi Jiuku Tianzun (male Daoist savior deity) and Jiutian Xuannü. Marked unattested per policy; flagged for potential removal or remap.

description: Igyō no danshi (異形の男子), 'the grotesque boy', is recorded in the Edo-period Chikuzen Bakemono Emaki: the armless son of Ōtomo Senzaemon, a retainer of Oka Castle in Bungo Province, born around 1842. He spoke from birth, had a scorching-hot body, breathed fire from his nostrils, and released a hitodama spirit-fire from his mouth — read as karmic retribution for his father's killing of animals.
research_notes: Verified against the Edo-period scroll account on yokai.com; the input's 'forest spirit with frost veil' description was fabricated and was replaced with the documented record.

description: Ippondatara (一本足) is a yōkai of the mountain districts of Kinki and Shikoku, especially Kumano in Wakayama: a being with a single leg and often a single eye that appears on mountain passes and roads during heavy rain, walking with a crashing, staggering gait. It is easily startled and flees when humans shout or throw things, though travelers who panic before it may be frightened to death.
research_notes: Verified against yokai.com and yokai databases; input's one-legged form, mountain habitat, and rain-time appearance confirmed. Added its fear of humans.

description: Imugi (이무기) is the immature dragon of Korean folklore: a great hornless serpent that failed to achieve full dragonhood, sometimes because it lacked the dragon jewel or could not climb the storm-ladder to heaven, and must wait a thousand years. Tales vary on whether it is benevolent or ominous, and 'imugi' sightings are also folk explanations for lake and river serpents.
research_notes: Verified against standard references; input's thousand-year wait and dragon-to-be status confirmed. Note the common spelling 'imoogi'.

description: Pixiu (貔貅) is an auspicious chimera of Chinese mythology, usually a winged, lion-like beast with a dragon's head, sometimes split into male (pí) and female (xiū). Because it feeds on wealth and has no anus, it is believed to gather and hold fortune without releasing it, making it a popular talisman for business and prosperity, worn as jade pendants and placed in homes and offices.
research_notes: Well-documented wealth creature; input's fortune-gathering nature and modern talisman role confirmed, with the no-anus motif added.

description: Qilin (麒麟) is the benevolent composite beast of Chinese tradition, with a dragon's head, deer's body, ox's tail, and fish-scale skin, sometimes bearing a single horn. It is said to appear only to mark the birth or reign of a sage and never to tread on living things, symbolizing peace, virtue, and good omens. It passed into Japan as the kirin and appears in Chinese New Year dances.
research_notes: Well-documented Chinese beast; input's composite form, sage-appearance, and benevolence confirmed. Kirin and dance traditions noted.

description: Dokkaebi (도깨비) are the goblins of Korean folklore: mischievous spirits said to form from objects stained with human blood or from old discarded household tools. They appear as horned, ugly beings who play pranks, trade using barley-straw or wooden money that turns back to leaves, and can be driven away with fire, pork, or red beans. Their magic club (dokkaebi bangmangi) is said to summon treasure.
research_notes: Well-documented Korean goblin; input's mischief and trickery confirmed. Origin-from-blood-soaked-objects, club, and red-bean/fire countermeasures added.

description: Huli jing (狐精) is the fox spirit of Chinese folklore: a fox that cultivates spiritual power over centuries, gaining the ability to shapeshift, usually into a beautiful woman who seduces and drains men's vitality. It appears in tales from the Six Dynasties, including Liaozhai Zhiyi. After a thousand years it grows nine tails, becoming the jiuwei hu; foxes may also be benevolent guardians.
research_notes: Well-documented Chinese fox spirit; input's shapeshifting, seduction, and centuries of cultivation confirmed. Nine-tail path and benevolence noted.

description: Haetae (해태) is the Korean chimera of justice and fire control, usually a lion-bodied, horned, scale-covered beast that swallows fire. It distinguishes right from wrong, goring the guilty, and protects against fire and calamity, which is why its statues guard palaces, government buildings, and Seoul's streets, including near the National Assembly. It descends from the Chinese xiezhi tradition.
research_notes: Well-documented Korean beast; input's fire control, justice, and protective statues confirmed, with the xiezhi lineage noted.

description: Obariyon (おばりよん) is a child-sized yōkai of Niigata Prefecture whose name comes from the local dialect phrase for 'give me a piggyback ride'. It leaps onto travelers' backs and grows heavier with every step, and may chew the scalp of its bearer, so some villages wore metal bowls as helmets. If carried home, the burden is found to be a sack of money, rewarding perseverance.
research_notes: Corrected a serious input error: the oil-licking lamp monster described in input is a different yōkai. Documented obariyon is the Niigata piggyback spirit that turns to gold; verified against yokai.com.

description: Oni (鬼) are the ogres or demons of Japanese folklore: large, fearsome beings with red, blue, or black skin, horns, sharp claws, and tiger-skin loincloths, often carrying iron clubs. They dwell in mountain fastnesses, punish the wicked, and cause disasters, yet also appear in protective roles. During Setsubun, people scatter roasted beans crying 'Oni wa soto!' to drive them from the home.
research_notes: Well-documented Japanese demons; input's horns, clubs, tiger-skin garments, and Setsubun expulsion all confirmed.

description: Nezha (哪吒) is the fiery third son of the Pagoda-Bearer Li Jing in Chinese mythology, central to Fengshen Yanyi and Journey to the West. Born after three years in the womb, he wields a fire-tipped spear, the cosmic ring Qiankun Quan, and the Wind-Fire Wheels he rides beneath his feet. He rebels, dies, and is reborn from a lotus as a powerful young guardian of heaven.
research_notes: Well-documented figure of Chinese mythology; input's weapons, lotus rebirth, and guardian role confirmed.
